This is the diffusion challenge and opportunity in a nutshell. Most people will probably get stuck with the use-cases that initially wowed them with AI, and have little incentive to move onto the next thing that will unlock another level of productivity. Even a large number of organizations can get stuck by being “satisfied” with AI gains, well before having full blown agents that can do any amount of work in the background or agent swarms that can take on complex, ambiguous problems. Much of this comes down to the technical complexity of implementing the architectures around this. Despite lots of effort to simplify the UXes, there’s still a lot of system work, data pipelines, MCPs, and security that needs to be worked through to get the most out of agents. But even when you’re done with that, you still need to redesign your workflow or process overall to get the full benefits from agents. This is why there’s so much opportunity to be an organization that figures this out early. It’s also why there’s going to be massive services and FDE opportunities right now as well, since most companies can’t do this on their own.

the race is not inevitable last year was fun. the models weren't that good yet, so i had to care about every detail. i pushed each thing until it had my thoughts and my designs. the tool helped. i did the driving. now the roles have flipped. we describe and watch things come back finished. we used to drive our dreams. more and more, we just watch. we set out to make things that give us more freedom. now we're racing toward something we might not be able to control. recursive self-improvement. intelligence building more intelligence, until we're no longer the ones who understand what's happening. that's the end game. the point where nobody is driving. the big labs are racing to get there first. the same system that cures a disease could design a new virus, or find every hole in the internet all at once. only the selected few with access could do anything about it. and somehow the possibility of losing everything we love becomes an argument for going faster. because someone else might get there first, and they might be less careful. because the company needs to survive. because too much money is already committed. everyone has a good reason to keep going toward an outcome nobody wants. so we call it inevitable. then nobody has to answer for it. but a race is made of decisions. someone approves the budget. someone decides the next model will help build the one after it. and we practice living inside the race long before we build it at the scale of civilization. sleep becomes recovery for work. friendship becomes a network. curiosity has to become a project before we let ourselves spend time on it. we get very rational. we start acting like the machines we're building. even our feelings have to defend themselves. why are you sad? is that useful? sometimes the feeling is how i begin to find out. there's a line in Zhuangzi. 大知閑閑，小知閒閒。 great knowledge is wide and unhurried. small knowledge is busy, always measuring. i don't think you can hurry your way to the first kind. i moved to Taipei to slow down and experience life. walking around Da'an. going into a cafe, or a cheap buffet. meeting new friends by accident, who brought me to a shisha bar. a 24-hour tea house, talking about life and the world we're in. getting closer to someone and feeling my heart beat faster... none of it was planned. none of it would show up in a report. i don't want to become so certain about where i'm going that nothing can reach me along the way. there's a tree in Zhuangzi too. a carpenter walks past a giant oak and calls it useless wood. that night the tree comes to him in a dream. the fruit trees you call useful get stripped every year, it says. being of no use is how i got to grow this big. the race looks at the world the way the carpenter looks at the tree. a night in a tea house is useless wood. so is a feeling you can't explain yet. that's most of what i want to protect. and there's a cook. after nineteen years his knife moves fast and easy, because he follows the openings between the joints. but at a hard knot, he slows down. when it's done, he stands there holding the knife and looks around. the people building these systems are some of the best cooks alive. this is the hardest knot anyone has come to. it's where a master slows down. we cloned a sheep thirty years ago, and we still don't clone people. we can slow down. change direction. decide something isn't worth building, even if it would make someone very rich. a probability can help us think about a risk. it can't decide what we have the right to risk on behalf of everyone else. i want what we build to stay answerable to the people who have to live with it. most of them will never be in the room. there are no stands in this race. whatever happens, happens to us. i'd like the people in that room to come out and sit for a while. it's harder to gamble with ordinary life once you've spent an evening in the middle of it. the tea house is open all night.

The greatest tragedy right now in Silicon Valley that NO one wants to talk about is how some startups are "reselling" compute and calling it revenue.. not inference, just straight up selling compute to other companies. And, no their primary business is NOT selling compute. In this era, where everyone wants to show high "annualized run rate" growth as that's the story that gets marked up, companies are now being even more creative in how to lump "revenue" into a month. It started with GMV-like revenue with low margins, then inference at negative gross margins and now straight up reselling compute. All lumped into a tidy "ARR". Naive investors will lap it up since it allows them to pass deals through IC, and seed investors will celebrate their markups - but zero shot this ends well.
